sampling-dist-two-proportions-s1.title: Bus riders in two school levels
sampling-dist-two-proportions-s1.text: A school district knows from its bus card records that 70% of its high school students and 55% of its middle school students ride a district bus at least once a week. A reporter takes independent random samples of 100 high school students and 80 middle school students and finds the sample proportion of bus riders in each, $\hat{p}_H$ and $\hat{p}_M$. (Invented data.)

sampling-dist-two-proportions-s2.title: 100 simulated differences in sample proportions
sampling-dist-two-proportions-s2.text: A teacher simulates two classes of 60 students each, where every student has a 0.40 chance of saying yes to a survey question, in both classes. The histogram shows 100 simulated values of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$, the difference in the two sample proportions, in bins 0.05 wide (each bin includes its left end).

plot.label: Histogram of 100 simulated differences in sample proportions in bins 0.05 wide, centered near 0, from about minus 0.3 to 0.25

items.q: What is the mean of the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}_H - \hat{p}_M$?

why.correct: The difference $\hat{p}_H - \hat{p}_M$ is an unbiased estimator of $p_H - p_M = 0.15$.
options: That averages the two proportions. The distribution of a difference is centered at the difference, $0.70 - 0.55$.
That divides 0.70 by 0.55. A difference is centered at $p_H - p_M$, a subtraction, not a ratio.
Zero would be the mean only if the two population proportions were equal. Here they differ by 0.15.
Right: the mean of a difference in sample proportions is the difference in the population proportions, $0.70 - 0.55 = 0.15$.

items.q: What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}_H - \hat{p}_M$? Give three decimal places.

mistakes.why: You added the two standard deviations. Add the variances (the parts inside the square roots), then take one square root.
You subtracted the variances. Variability adds up even when you subtract the statistics, so add the two parts under the square root.

items.q: Which check shows that the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}_H - \hat{p}_M$ is approximately normal?

why.correct: Approximate normality needs at least 10 expected successes and 10 expected failures in each sample.
options: Proportions above 0.5 do not make a shape normal. The counts $n p$ and $n(1 - p)$ in each sample must reach 10.
Random selection lets you generalize, but it says nothing about the shape. The shape comes from the large counts condition.
Right: the large counts condition is checked for both samples, successes and failures, four counts in all.
Comparing $n$ with 30 is a rule for sample means. For proportions, check the four counts $n_1 p_1$, $n_1(1 - p_1)$, $n_2 p_2$, $n_2(1 - p_2)$ against 10.
Both population proportions, 0.70 and 0.55, are above 0.5
Both samples were selected at random from the district
The combined sample size, $100 + 80 = 180$, is at least 30

items.q: What is the probability that $\hat{p}_H - \hat{p}_M$ is 0.05 or less? Give four decimal places.

why.correct: $z = \frac{0.05 - 0.15}{0.072} = -1.39$, so $P(\hat{p}_H - \hat{p}_M \le 0.05) = 0.0826$ (the area to the left of $z$ under the standard normal curve).

mistakes.why: That uses the sum of the two standard deviations (0.101) as the spread. The standard deviation of the difference is 0.072: add variances, not standard deviations.
That centers the distribution at 0. The sampling distribution is centered at $p_H - p_M = 0.15$.

items.q: The reporter finds $\hat{p}_H - \hat{p}_M = 0.02$. What does the sampling distribution say about this result?

why.correct: Compare the result with the sampling distribution: how many standard deviations from the mean is it, and how often does it happen?
options: One unusual sample is not proof. It is surprising if the records are right, which is a reason to look closer, not a certainty.
Sample differences vary from sample to sample. The value 0.15 is the center of that variation, not the only possible result.
Right: $z = \frac{0.02 - 0.15}{0.072} = -1.80$, and the area below it is about 0.036. Such a small difference is rare when the true difference is 0.15.
Positive is not enough. A difference of 0.02 sits 1.8 standard deviations below the mean of 0.15.
It shows that the district records are wrong
It is impossible, because the difference has to be 0.15
It is unusual: a difference of 0.02 or less happens in about 4% of samples like these
It is typical, because 0.02 is a positive difference like 0.15

items.q: Why is the histogram centered near 0?

options: Sample size affects the spread and the shape. The center comes from $p_1 - p_2$.
The number of trials changes how smooth the histogram looks, not where it is centered.
The center is the difference of the two proportions, $0.40 - 0.40 = 0$, not either proportion.
Right: the difference in sample proportions is centered at the difference in the true proportions, which is 0 here.
Each class has more than 30 students
The teacher ran an even number of trials
A proportion of 0.40 is fairly close to 0 on this scale
The true proportions are equal, so $p_1 - p_2 = 0$

items.q: In how many of the 100 trials was the difference 0.15 or more, and what does that estimate?

why.correct: A simulated probability is the count of trials at or beyond the value, over the number of trials.
options: The simulation assumed the proportions were equal. It estimates how often a difference that large happens under that assumption, not the chance the assumption is true.
That counts the trials below 0.15. The question asks for 0.15 or more.
Right: add the heights of the bars from 0.15 up (6) and divide by the 100 trials.
The number of trials has to be read from the bars. A cutoff value does not tell you how many trials lie beyond it.
6 trials, so about 0.06 is the probability that the two true proportions are equal
94 trials, so a difference of 0.15 or more happens in most samples like these
6 trials; about 0.06 estimates the chance of a difference this large
15 trials, because the value 0.15 stands for 15 out of each 100 trials

items.q: The 100 simulated differences have a standard deviation of 0.088. Which formula value is this an estimate of?

why.correct: For independent samples the variances add: $\sigma^2 = \frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}$.
options: That is the standard deviation of one sample proportion. A difference of two independent sample proportions varies more: add both variances.
Putting both classes in one sample of 120 gives the spread of one proportion, not of a difference of two.
That is the variance. Take the square root to get a standard deviation.
Right: the simulation estimates the standard deviation of the sampling distribution, and the formula gives it exactly.

items.q: The teacher repeats the simulation with 240 students in each class instead of 60. How does the new histogram compare?

why.correct: Quadrupling both sample sizes halves the standard deviation of the difference.
options: The center is $p_1 - p_2 = 0$, whatever the sample size.
The spread depends on the sample sizes as well as the proportions. Larger samples vary less.
Four times the sample size divides the variance by 4, but the standard deviation, its square root, only by 2.
Right: each variance is divided by 4, so the standard deviation is divided by $\sqrt{4} = 2$. The center stays at 0.
A center four times farther from 0
The same spread, because the proportions are still 0.40
About the same center, with about a quarter of the spread
About the same center, with about half the spread

items.q: A survey asks 200 married couples whether each partner exercises weekly, and compares $\hat{p}_{\text{wives}} - \hat{p}_{\text{husbands}}$. Why should the standard deviation formula for a difference of two sample proportions not be used here?

why.correct: The variance of a difference is the sum of the variances only for independent samples.
options: Equal sample sizes are fine. The problem is that the samples are linked couple by couple.
There is no such size rule. The formula needs two independent samples, and these are paired.
Right: the formula adds two variances, which works only when the two samples are independent. Partners in one household are linked.
Whether a person exercises weekly is categorical (yes or no), so proportions are right. The samples are the issue.
The two sample sizes are equal, at 200 people each
The survey has fewer than 1,000 people taking part in it
The samples are linked: each wife is paired with her husband
Exercise is a quantitative variable, not a categorical one

items.q: Independent random samples of 100 high school students and 80 middle school students are drawn without replacement. Which statement checks the 10% condition?

why.correct: Sampling without replacement: each sample is less than 10% of its population, so the observations are close enough to independent.
options: That is part of the large counts condition, which is about shape. The 10% condition is about sampling without replacement.
That checks the random condition. The 10% condition is about the size of each sample compared with its population.
Right: the 10% condition is checked for each sample against its own population.
The 10% condition compares each sample with its population, and the sample must be smaller than 10% of it.
At least 10 students in each of the two samples ride the bus
The samples were chosen at random from two separate lists of students
Each sample is less than 10% of the students at its own school level
100 and 80 are each at least 10% of the combined sample of 180

items.q: In a large city, 35% of adults under 30 and 25% of adults 30 or older use a bike share at least once a month. Independent random samples of 250 younger adults and 200 older adults are taken. Write the expression for the standard deviation of $\hat{p}_{\text{young}} - \hat{p}_{\text{old}}$, then give its value to three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That adds two standard deviations. Put both variance terms under one square root.
Subtracting the statistics still adds variability: the two terms under the square root are added.
That treats the difference 0.10 as one proportion from one sample. Each group keeps its own proportion and its own sample size.

items.q: For the bike share samples, the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}_{\text{young}} - \hat{p}_{\text{old}}$ is approximately normal with mean 0.10 and standard deviation 0.043. What is the probability that the sample difference is greater than 0.15? Give four decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is the area to the left of 0.15. "Greater than" asks for the area to the right: subtract from 1.
That centers the distribution at 0. Its mean is $p_1 - p_2 = 0.10$.

items.q: Which change makes the standard deviation of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ smaller, with the population proportions kept the same?

why.correct: Both terms $\frac{p(1-p)}{n}$ shrink as their $n$ grows.
options: The question keeps the proportions fixed. The spread is lowered by larger samples.
One combined sample gives one proportion. It no longer measures a difference between two groups.
Switching the order changes the sign of the mean, not the spread. The variances add either way.
Right: each variance term has its sample size in the denominator, so larger samples shrink both terms.
Using a larger difference between the populations
Combining the two samples into one
Subtracting in the other order, $\hat{p}_2 - \hat{p}_1$
Taking larger samples from both populations

items.q: A clinic compares two rare side effects: 5% of patients on drug A and 8% on drug B have one. It takes independent random samples of 40 patients on each drug. Which condition fails for treating $\hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_B$ as approximately normal?

why.correct: Each of $n_1 p_1$, $n_1(1-p_1)$, $n_2 p_2$, $n_2(1-p_2)$ must be at least 10.
options: A small sample makes the 10% condition easier to meet. The problem is too few expected successes.
Right: with rare outcomes and small samples, too few expected successes make the distribution skewed.
Two separate random samples of patients are independent even if the drugs treat the same illness.
Rare outcomes do not make a sample nonrandom. They make the large counts condition fail.
The 10% condition, because 40 patients is a small sample
Large counts: $40(0.05) = 2$ and $40(0.08) = 3.2$ are below 10
Independence, because both of the drugs are used for the same illness
Random, because side effects are rare

items.q: A student says, "The standard deviation of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is the standard deviation of $\hat{p}_1$ minus the standard deviation of $\hat{p}_2$." What is wrong with this?

why.correct: $\sigma_{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2} = \sqrt{\sigma^2_{\hat{p}_1} + \sigma^2_{\hat{p}_2}}$, which is larger than either standard deviation.
options: Right: each sample brings its own chance error, and the two errors do not cancel, so the spread of a difference is larger than either one.
If that were right, two samples with equal spreads would give a difference with no spread at all, which is not what happens.
Multiplying has no basis here. For independent samples the variances add.
An average would make the difference less variable than one of the samples. The spread of a difference is larger than either.
Variability from two independent samples adds, so the variances are added
Nothing; a difference of statistics has a difference of standard deviations
The standard deviations should be multiplied
The standard deviations should be averaged

items.q: Two independent random samples of 300 come from populations with $p_1 = 0.50$ and $p_2 = 0.50$. About how far from 0 is a typical value of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$?

why.correct: The standard deviation is the typical distance of the statistic from its mean.
options: Right: $\sqrt{\frac{0.5(0.5)}{300} + \frac{0.5(0.5)}{300}} = 0.041$, a typical distance from the mean of 0.
That is one of the proportions. The question asks how much the difference varies.
That is the variance, $\frac{0.25}{300} + \frac{0.25}{300}$, before the square root.
That is the standard deviation of one sample proportion, 0.029. A difference of two varies more.
About 0.04
About 0.50
About 0.0017
About 0.03
